_comment: DRAFT -- NOT live. Old Testament levels 19-21 of 23: the cycle of the Judges, Saul and the anointing of David, and David as king bringing the ark to Jerusalem. 2 Samuel 6:9 and 6:11 are already reviewed and used here; all other Scripture references are new and flagged by onramp_tool.py check for translation verification before shipping.

questions.prompt: What recurring pattern shapes the book of Judges, across many different leaders?
choices: Israel sins, is oppressed, cries out, and is delivered by a judge
Israel conquers steadily with no setbacks at all
A single dynasty rules continuously through the whole period
Foreign nations govern Israel without any resistance
questions.correctAnswer: Israel sins, is oppressed, cries out, and is delivered by a judge
questions.explanation: The cycle repeats again and again with different names attached -- Deborah, Gideon, Samson -- but the same shape every time: unfaithfulness, oppression, a cry for help, and a deliverer raised up.
questions.hint: The same four-part shape repeats with different judges each time.

citations.quote: the LORD raised up judges to deliver them... Yet whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD would be with him and save them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived.

questions.prompt: True or False: During the time of the Judges, deliverance from oppression lasted only as long as that particular judge was alive.
questions.explanation: True, and this is what keeps the cycle turning: relief comes with each judge, but it is not permanent. Israel returns to unfaithfulness once the judge who rescued them has died.
questions.hint: Consider what happens once each individual judge dies.

citations.quote: the LORD raised up judges to deliver them... Yet whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD would be with him and save them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived.

questions.prompt: The book of Judges closes with a telling line: 'In those days there was no ____ in Israel; everyone did as they saw fit.'
questions.explanation: The book's own closing verdict names what it thinks is missing -- not simply better judges, but a king. That sentence is what the next level's story directly answers.
questions.hint: It names the office Israel will ask for in the next level.

citations.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

questions.prompt: According to the book's own closing line, what marked the period when there was no king in Israel?
choices: Everyone did what was right in their own eyes
The Law was kept faithfully by everyone
The twelve tribes were perfectly united
No conflict with neighboring nations occurred
questions.correctAnswer: Everyone did what was right in their own eyes
questions.explanation: Without a king, without a single covenant-keeping authority holding the tribes together, the book's own diagnosis is that Israel's cycle of unfaithfulness had no check on it.
questions.hint: The judgment concerns a lack of shared authority, not a lack of individual effort.

citations.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

questions.prompt: True or False: The judges of this period were meant to be permanent kings ruling by hereditary right.
questions.explanation: False. Judges were raised up by God for a specific deliverance, not installed as a permanent dynasty -- which is exactly the gap the closing verse of the book points to.
questions.hint: Consider whether a judge's role was passed down to their children as a rule.

citations.quote: the LORD raised up judges to deliver them... Yet whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD would be with him and save them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived.

questions.prompt: Match each stage of the Judges cycle to what happens in it.

pairs.right: Turns from the LORD toward other gods
A foreign power gains control over Israel
Calls on the LORD for deliverance
Delivers Israel only as long as they live

questions.explanation: This cycle repeats through the whole book with different names attached to the fourth stage each time. The pattern itself, not any one judge, is the real subject of Judges.
questions.hint: Read the four stages as one repeating cycle, not four separate events.

citations.quote: the LORD raised up judges to deliver them... Yet whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD would be with him and save them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived.

questions.prompt: How does the period of the Judges connect to the choice Joshua set before Israel at the end of the last level?
choices: It shows what happens when each generation fails to choose faithfully
It shows the covenant was permanently secured after Joshua's challenge
It has no real connection to Joshua's challenge at all
It shows Israel choosing faithfully without any relapse
questions.correctAnswer: It shows what happens when each generation fails to choose faithfully
questions.explanation: Joshua warned that belonging to the covenant is not automatic. The book of Judges is that warning playing out in real time -- generation after generation failing to renew the choice for themselves.
questions.hint: Recall what Joshua said about each generation needing to choose for itself.

citations.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

questions.prompt: True or False: The cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance is the same shape this topic already traced after the golden calf.
questions.explanation: True. Failure met by mercy, not abandonment -- the same rhythm named at the golden calf repeats through the entire period of the Judges, generation after generation.
questions.hint: This same rhythm was named explicitly at an earlier point in this topic.

citations.quote: the LORD raised up judges to deliver them... Yet whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD would be with him and save them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived.

questions.prompt: Judges says the LORD saved Israel from their enemies as long as the ____ lived.
questions.explanation: Deliverance in this period is tied to one person's life. It is exactly this instability that the book's closing verse points to as the real problem.
questions.hint: The deliverance lasted only as long as this one person was alive.

citations.quote: the LORD raised up judges to deliver them... Yet whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD would be with him and save them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived.

questions.prompt: What real problem is the book of Judges pointing to when it says Israel had no king?
choices: A lack of stable, covenant-faithful leadership across generations
A shortage of skilled military commanders only
A lack of a central location for worship alone
A dispute over which tribe should hold the most land
questions.correctAnswer: A lack of stable, covenant-faithful leadership across generations
questions.explanation: Judges are temporary and personal; the office the book is missing is one that could hold the covenant steady across generations, not just win one battle at a time.
questions.hint: Consider what a judge could not provide that a king might.

citations.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in their own eyes.

questions.prompt: When Samuel is sent to anoint Israel's next king from among Jesse's sons, what does God tell him not to judge by?
choices: Outward appearance
Age and seniority
Wealth and property
Prior military experience
questions.explanation: Samuel is drawn to the oldest, most impressive-looking son first. God's correction reframes the whole selection: appearance is what a man sees, but the LORD looks into the heart.
questions.hint: Samuel's first instinct is drawn to someone's looks.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: True or False: David is anointed by Samuel even though he is the youngest of Jesse's sons, out tending sheep.
questions.explanation: True. David is not even brought in from the field until every other son has been passed over -- the youngest, the least considered, is the one chosen.
questions.hint: He is not even present when his brothers are first presented to Samuel.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: Samuel is told: 'God does not see as a mortal... the LORD looks into the ____.'
questions.explanation: The standard God uses to choose a king has nothing to do with the standards Israel would later demand -- height, appearance, the look of a warrior. What God sees is not visible at all.
questions.hint: What a human being cannot see directly, but God can.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: What was David's occupation at the moment Samuel came to anoint him?
choices: Shepherding his father's flock
Serving as a soldier in Saul's army
Working as a scribe in the local town
Already ruling as a minor official
questions.explanation: The one anointed to shepherd Israel is, at the moment of his anointing, literally a shepherd of sheep -- an image Scripture will return to again and again when it speaks of David and of the greater king to come.
questions.hint: The occupation itself becomes a lasting image for the kind of king he will be.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: True or False: David is anointed king by Samuel while Saul is still reigning as king.
questions.explanation: True. David's anointing comes years before he actually takes the throne -- he is chosen long before he reigns, and lives through Saul's continued kingship, and Saul's hostility toward him, in the meantime.
questions.hint: Consider the gap between being anointed and actually becoming king.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: Match each figure in the anointing account to their role.

pairs.right: Sent by God to anoint the next king
The youngest, chosen for his heart
What David was tending when he was chosen

questions.explanation: Every detail works against expectation: the prophet's own first instinct is wrong, the obvious candidates are passed over, and the one chosen is not even present until called.
questions.hint: Notice how each figure defies what would normally be expected.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: Why does even the prophet Samuel need to be corrected in choosing the next king?
choices: Because even a prophet can default to human standards of judgment
Because Samuel secretly opposed David from the start
Because Samuel had never met Jesse's family before
Because Samuel was testing Jesse's sons deliberately
questions.correctAnswer: Because even a prophet can default to human standards of judgment
questions.explanation: Samuel's own instinct, on seeing the eldest son, is to assume this must be the one. God's correction is aimed at Samuel himself, not only at Israel -- no one is exempt from needing this reminder.
questions.hint: Samuel's own first reaction needs to be corrected.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: True or False: The standard God uses to choose David directly contrasts with what Israel had originally wanted in a king.
questions.explanation: True. Israel had wanted a king who looked the part; God chooses one whose heart is right instead -- a contrast this level makes as pointed as it can.
questions.hint: Consider what kind of king Israel originally asked for, versus who God actually chooses.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: Samuel is told not to judge David's older brother by his appearance or his lofty ____.
questions.explanation: Physical impressiveness is named specifically as the wrong measure. Whatever made this brother look like an obvious king is exactly what God says does not matter here.
questions.hint: It refers to how tall or physically impressive someone appears.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: How does David's anointing as a shepherd-boy connect forward to Luke's Gospel, which this topic reached at level 6?
choices: The angel tells Mary her son will receive the throne of David
It has no real connection to anything in Luke's Gospel
David's shepherding is repeated literally by Jesus as an occupation
Luke never mentions David anywhere in his Gospel
questions.correctAnswer: The angel tells Mary her son will receive the throne of David
questions.explanation: The shepherd-boy anointed in a field becomes the reference point for a promise made centuries later at the Annunciation -- 'the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.'
questions.hint: Recall the announcement made to Mary earlier in this topic.

citations.quote: the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will rule over the house of Jacob forever
Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: When David brings the ark of the covenant toward Jerusalem, what is his first reaction after a man dies touching it?
choices: Fear -- he asks how the ark could ever come to him
Anger at the man who died for interfering
Indifference, and he continues the procession at once
He abandons the plan to bring the ark to Jerusalem forever
questions.correctAnswer: Fear -- he asks how the ark could ever come to him
questions.explanation: David's fear here is not mere caution -- it is reverence for something genuinely holy, the same reverence Moses was shown at the burning bush, now facing the king himself.
questions.hint: His response is one of reverence, not simple caution or anger.

citations.quote: David feared the Lord that day and said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'

questions.prompt: True or False: David leaves the ark in the house of Obed-edom for three months before finally bringing it to Jerusalem.
questions.explanation: True. David's fear leads him to pause the procession entirely -- the ark rests in Obed-edom's house for three months before David finally continues bringing it up to the city.
questions.hint: David's fear leads him to pause the procession for a real length of time.

citations.quote: The ark of the Lord remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months.

questions.prompt: David asks: 'How can the ark of the Lord come to ____?'
questions.explanation: Even as king, David does not treat the ark's presence as something he is simply entitled to. The question is genuine reverence, not rhetorical hesitation.
questions.hint: David is asking about himself specifically, not about the ark in general.

citations.quote: David feared the Lord that day and said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'

questions.prompt: Why does bringing the ark to Jerusalem matter so much for David's kingship?
choices: It makes Jerusalem the center of Israel's worship, not merely its politics
It has purely military significance for defending the city
It replaces the covenant given earlier at Sinai
It was required before David could be anointed at all
questions.correctAnswer: It makes Jerusalem the center of Israel's worship, not merely its politics
questions.explanation: David is not simply relocating a religious object to his own capital for prestige. Bringing the ark to Jerusalem unites the political center of the kingdom with the place where God's presence dwells among his people.
questions.hint: Consider what the ark represents, beyond being an object.

citations.quote: The ark of the Lord remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months.

questions.prompt: True or False: David's fear of the ark shows the same reverence for holiness this topic first named at the burning bush.
questions.explanation: True. Moses removed his sandals before holy ground; David pauses an entire procession, three months long, before holy presence. The reverence is the same, even generations apart.
questions.hint: Recall the instruction Moses received before the burning bush.

citations.quote: David feared the Lord that day and said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'

questions.prompt: Match each moment of David's kingship to what it establishes.

pairs.right: Chosen for his heart, not his stature
Reverence for what is genuinely holy
Worship and kingship united in one city

questions.explanation: David's whole kingship, from his anointing to this procession, is marked by the same thing: a real regard for what is God's, not a king's casual claim on it.
questions.hint: Trace how each moment builds David's specific character as king.

citations.quote: David feared the Lord that day and said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'
Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.

questions.prompt: What does David's kingship, taken as a whole so far, answer from the period of the Judges?
choices: A single, covenant-faithful leadership that can hold Israel together
A return to having no central leadership at all
A king chosen purely for his military record
A permanent removal of any further need for repentance
questions.correctAnswer: A single, covenant-faithful leadership that can hold Israel together
questions.explanation: Judges ended with the diagnosis that Israel had no king, and everyone did as they saw fit. David -- chosen for his heart, reverent before what is holy -- is the answer this topic has been building toward since that verse.
questions.hint: Recall exactly what the book of Judges said Israel lacked.

citations.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in their own eyes.
David feared the Lord that day and said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'

questions.prompt: True or False: Once the ark reaches Jerusalem, this topic's typological thread of covenant, kingship, and worship converges in one place.
questions.explanation: True. Everything traced since Abraham -- covenant, promised land, the Law, a king after God's own heart -- now converges physically in one city, on David's throne, around the ark.
questions.hint: Consider how many earlier threads of this topic meet at this single moment.

citations.quote: The ark of the Lord remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months.

questions.prompt: The ark remained in the house of ____ the Gittite for three months.
questions.explanation: A specific man, a specific household, named directly in the text -- Scripture is precise about where the ark rested during David's hesitation, not vague about the delay.
questions.hint: It is a specific man's name, given directly in the text.

citations.quote: The ark of the Lord remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months.

questions.prompt: Looking at levels 19 through 21 together, what has this topic's answer to the crisis of the Judges finally become?
choices: A king chosen for his heart, reverent before God, uniting worship and rule
A return to rule by many independent judges again
A king who rules by force with no regard for the covenant
A permanent solution requiring no further trust in God
questions.correctAnswer: A king chosen for his heart, reverent before God, uniting worship and rule
questions.explanation: Everything this stretch has covered -- the anointing, the fear before the ark, the ark's arrival in Jerusalem -- answers the exact gap Judges named. David is not a perfect end point, as the next level will show, but he is a real answer to what was missing.
questions.hint: Weigh what the anointing and the ark's arrival together have accomplished.

citations.quote: Do not judge from his appearance or from his lofty stature... God does not see as a mortal, who sees the appearance. The LORD looks into the heart.
David feared the Lord that day and said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'
